title: Immune Responses in Hematologic Disease
subject: Hematology (HEME)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter explains what happens when the immune system turns on blood cells, on transfused blood, or on the clotting system, and what happens when the spleen is lost. It covers autoimmune hemolysis and the Coombs test, hypersensitivity classification, transfusion reactions, heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, antiphospholipid syndrome, Epstein-Barr virus in B cells, and infection after asplenia. Board questions give a smear, a laboratory pattern, or a time course and ask for the antibody, effector, or organ responsible. The recurring idea is that antibody class, temperature, antigen location, and Fc receptor engagement decide whether the result is hemolysis, thrombosis, or infection.
prerequisites: Antibody classes, Fc receptors, and the classical complement pathway
Gell and Coombs hypersensitivity types I to IV
Red cell destruction: intravascular versus extravascular hemolysis and their laboratory markers
Platelet activation and the coagulation cascade, including the PT and PTT
B and T cell activation, T cell help, and class switching

connections.to: Hemolytic anemias (HE chapters on red cell disorders)
connections.how: Immune hemolysis must be separated from membrane, enzyme, and hemoglobin defects, and the direct Coombs test is the dividing line.
HIT and antiphospholipid syndrome show that antibodies can drive clotting, not bleeding, by activating platelets, endothelium, and monocytes.
Hypersensitivity types, complement, Fc receptors, and T-independent versus T-dependent antigens explain every disorder in this chapter.
Mycoplasma pneumoniae, EBV, and encapsulated bacteria link infection to cold agglutinins, lymphoma, and post-splenectomy sepsis.
SLE causes warm hemolysis and antiphospholipid antibodies, and cryoglobulinemia causes immune complex glomerulonephritis.

sections.title: Warm autoimmune hemolysis, cold agglutinin disease, and the Coombs test

blocks.text: In autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA) the patient makes antibodies against their own red cell antigens. Both forms produce the general signs of hemolysis: anemia, reticulocytosis, raised lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and unconjugated bilirubin, and low haptoglobin. They differ in antibody class, which sets the temperature at which the antibody binds.
Warm AIHA

Warm autoantibodies are IgG and bind best at 37 °C (98.6 °F), often to Rh-related membrane proteins. IgG activates complement poorly, so the main effector is the splenic macrophage, whose Fc gamma receptors grip the IgG-coated cell and remove a piece of membrane. The cell reseals with less surface area for its volume and becomes a spherocyte, which is rigid and is trapped in the splenic cords on later passes. Hemolysis is therefore extravascular, and splenomegaly is common. About half of cases are idiopathic; the rest are secondary to autoimmune disease (SLE), lymphoid neoplasms (CLL), or drugs, which may act as haptens or induce true autoantibodies.
Cold agglutinin disease

Cold agglutinins are IgM, usually against the I antigen, and bind in cooler blood of the fingers, toes, ears, and nose, generally below about 30 °C (86 °F). Because IgM is a pentamer it bridges neighboring cells, causing agglutination, and a single bound molecule activates C1. On rewarming the IgM detaches but C3b remains, so Kupffer cells in the liver clear C3b-coated cells (mostly extravascular), while some cells complete the cascade and lyse intravascularly. Acrocyanosis and hemolysis worsen in the cold. Transient polyclonal cold agglutinins follow Mycoplasma pneumoniae (anti-I) and EBV mononucleosis (anti-i); chronic disease is usually driven by a clonal B cell population making monoclonal IgM.

blocks.text: Reading the Coombs test

The direct Coombs test asks whether antibody or complement is already on the patient's red cells. Washed cells are mixed with anti-human globulin, an antibody against human IgG or C3; if the red cells are coated, the reagent bridges them and they agglutinate. The indirect test asks whether free antibody is in the serum: the serum is first incubated with reagent red cells and then tested the same way, which is how antibody screens and crossmatches work. A positive direct test means immune coating, whether autoimmune (AIHA), alloimmune (transfusion reaction, hemolytic disease of the newborn), or drug related; it does not prove hemolysis, because a small fraction of healthy people test positive.

blocks.title: Worked example: interpreting a positive direct Coombs test
blocks.text: A 25-year-old with a week of cough and patchy infiltrates develops anemia, raised LDH, and low haptoglobin. The analyzer reports a falsely high MCV because clumps are counted as single large cells. The direct Coombs is C3 positive and IgG negative. Step one: the markers confirm hemolysis, and the positive direct test shows an immune cause. Step two: C3 without IgG means the antibody detached after fixing complement, which fits IgM. Step three: agglutination and a respiratory infection point to Mycoplasma-induced cold agglutinins (anti-I). IgG with spherocytes in SLE would instead indicate warm AIHA.

blocks.predict: Why is the direct Coombs test in cold agglutinin disease positive for C3 but not IgM?
blocks.explain: IgM binds weakly and detaches on warming and washing, but the C3 it fixed stays covalently bound to the membrane.
blocks.check: The cold agglutinin mechanism and the Coombs table row.

blocks.text: Hypersensitivity type is decided by where the antibody meets its antigen and which effector it recruits. In type II reactions the antigen is fixed on a cell or in matrix, so the antibody marks that cell for destruction by complement, by Fc receptor phagocytosis, or by antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity. In type III reactions the antigen is soluble; antibody and antigen form immune complexes that circulate and deposit in vessel walls and glomeruli, where complement and neutrophils damage tissue that was never the target. Blood disorders fall mainly into these two groups.

blocks.title: Hypersensitivity types with hematologic examples
rows: Preformed IgE on mast cells, immediate mediator release
IgG or IgM against a cell-bound antigen; complement, phagocytosis, ADCC
Acute and delayed hemolytic transfusion reactions, AIHA, hemolytic disease of the newborn, immune thrombocytopenia
Soluble antigen and antibody form complexes that deposit and fix complement
blocks.caption: Hemolytic disorders are type II; cryoglobulinemia is the main hematologic type III disorder.

blocks.text: Type II: three red cell examples

In the acute hemolytic transfusion reaction, the recipient's preformed IgM anti-A or anti-B (isohemagglutinins, made in infancy after exposure to similar carbohydrate antigens on gut bacteria) bind incompatible donor cells and activate complement to the membrane attack complex, so lysis is intravascular. In AIHA the target is self. In hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn (HDFN), maternal IgG crosses the placenta, carried by the neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn), and coats fetal red cells, which are removed in the fetal spleen. IgM cannot cross the placenta, which is why naturally occurring anti-A and anti-B usually spare the fetus.

blocks.title: Rh hemolytic disease of the newborn
steps: RhD-negative mother carries RhD-positive fetus
Fetal cells enter maternal blood, usually at delivery
Mother makes IgM, then memory B cells
Next RhD-positive pregnancy: anamnestic IgG anti-D
IgG crosses placenta via FcRn and coats fetal cells
Fetal anemia, hydrops; neonatal jaundice and kernicterus risk
blocks.caption: Sensitization usually spares the first pregnancy; later pregnancies are affected by IgG anti-D.

blocks.text: Severe fetal anemia causes high-output heart failure, and extramedullary hematopoiesis in the liver reduces albumin synthesis, together producing hydrops fetalis. Before birth the placenta clears bilirubin; after birth the immature liver cannot conjugate it fast enough, and unconjugated bilirubin can cross the blood-brain barrier (kernicterus). ABO incompatibility is more common but milder: mothers who are group O can make IgG anti-A and anti-B, it can affect a first pregnancy, and fetal A and B antigens are weakly expressed and also present on other tissues that absorb antibody.
Type III: cryoglobulinemia

Cryoglobulins are immunoglobulins that precipitate below 37 °C (98.6 °F) and redissolve on warming. Type I is a single monoclonal immunoglobulin (myeloma, Waldenström macroglobulinemia) and causes mainly hyperviscosity and vessel occlusion. Mixed types II and III contain IgM rheumatoid factor (monoclonal in type II, polyclonal in type III) bound to polyclonal IgG; these complexes deposit in small vessels, consume complement (C4 especially low), and cause leukocytoclastic vasculitis with palpable purpura, arthralgia, membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, and neuropathy. Chronic hepatitis C is the leading cause, because persistent antigen stimulates B cell clonal expansion; Sjögren syndrome and SLE are others. The blood must be kept at 37 °C until the serum is separated, or the cryoglobulin precipitates with the clot and the test is falsely negative.

sections.title: Transfusion reactions by mechanism, timing, and findings

blocks.text: Transfusion reactions are sorted by three questions: what in the unit or the recipient caused it, how soon it began, and whether red cells were destroyed. Only hemolytic reactions show hemolysis and a positive direct Coombs test.

Fever, chills, flank pain, hypotension, red urine (hemoglobinuria), positive direct Coombs, DIC, acute kidney injury
Anamnestic IgG against minor antigens (Kidd, Rh, Kell, Duffy) from prior transfusion or pregnancy; extravascular

Cytokines from donor white cells in storage, or recipient anti-HLA against donor leukocytes
Rise of at least 1 °C (1.8 °F) to 38 °C (100.4 °F) or more, chills; no hemolysis; diagnosis of exclusion

Hypotension, bronchospasm, angioedema, urticaria; no fever
Bacteria in the unit; endotoxin and bacteremia

blocks.caption: Timing and the presence or absence of hemolysis separate most reactions.

blocks.text: The acute hemolytic reaction is the most dangerous and is usually caused by a clerical or identification error. Complement activation releases the anaphylatoxins C3a and C5a and inflammatory cytokines, producing fever and hypotension. Free hemoglobin scavenges nitric oxide, adding vasoconstriction, while hypotension and pigment injure the tubules. Exposure of tissue factor and phospholipid on damaged cells can trigger disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). Plasma turns pink and haptoglobin falls.

The delayed hemolytic reaction occurs in a patient previously sensitized whose antibody had fallen below detection, so the pretransfusion screen was negative; Kidd antibodies are notorious for this. Re-exposure triggers a memory IgG response, and coated cells are cleared by splenic macrophages. Febrile nonhemolytic reactions are the most common and are reduced by removing white cells before storage (leukoreduction), which explains their cytokine mechanism.

Anaphylaxis follows exposure to a plasma protein the recipient lacks. Selective IgA deficiency is the most common primary immunodeficiency, and a minority of affected people have anti-IgA antibodies; the reaction appears within seconds and lacks fever, which distinguishes it from hemolysis and sepsis. Septic reactions are most often from platelets, stored at about 20 to 24 °C (68 to 75 °F), which allows skin flora such as staphylococci to grow; refrigerated red cells can carry Yersinia enterocolitica, which grows at cold temperatures and thrives on iron. Transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI) follows a two-hit model: illness primes neutrophils that sequester in the lung, and donor antibodies, often from plasma of women with many pregnancies, activate them to release proteases and oxidants that make capillaries leak. It must be separated from circulatory overload, which is hydrostatic and comes with hypertension and raised natriuretic peptides.

blocks.title: Worked example: sorting a reaction by timing
blocks.text: A woman with three prior pregnancies receives 2 units of red cells after surgery. Her antibody screen was negative. Seven days later her hemoglobin has fallen from 10 to 8 g/dL, bilirubin is mildly raised, the smear shows spherocytes, and the direct Coombs is newly IgG positive. Step one: hemolysis began days later, which excludes the acute reactions. Step two: IgG with spherocytes means extravascular clearance. Step three: a delay of days in a previously pregnant patient fits an anamnestic response to a minor antigen that had dropped below detection. This is a delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction, and a repeat screen will often now identify the antibody, for example anti-Jka (Kidd).

Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) is an immune reaction in which antibodies cause clotting rather than bleeding. The antigen is created when heparin meets platelet factor 4 (PF4), a positively charged chemokine released from platelet alpha granules. Heparin is a long, negatively charged polysaccharide, and when it binds several PF4 molecules at suitable ratios they form large complexes in which PF4 changes shape and exposes new epitopes. Some patients make IgG against these neoepitopes.

blocks.title: The HIT amplification loop
steps: Heparin binds PF4, exposing a new epitope
IgG binds heparin and PF4 complexes on platelets
Fc portions cross-link platelet Fc gamma RIIa
Platelets activate, aggregate, and shed procoagulant microparticles
Alpha granules release more PF4
More PF4 forms more antigen with heparin
blocks.caption: Each round of activation releases more PF4, so the antigen and the platelet activation reinforce each other.

blocks.text: The key step is the Fc gamma RIIa receptor on platelets. The IgG binds the complex on the platelet surface, and its Fc portion engages Fc receptors on the same and neighboring platelets, which delivers an activating signal. Activated platelets aggregate, release more PF4, and shed microparticles that provide phospholipid for clotting factor complexes. The same immune complexes activate monocytes, which express tissue factor, and bind PF4 attached to endothelial heparan sulfate, injuring the endothelium. The combined result is a burst of thrombin generation. Antibody-coated platelets are also removed by macrophages, so the platelet count falls while clots form.
Timing and findings

Because a new IgG response must develop, the count typically falls 5 to 10 days after heparin is started. If the patient received heparin within about the previous 100 days, circulating antibody may already be present and the fall can begin within 24 hours. The drop is usually more than 50% from baseline, with a median nadir of about 50,000 to 60,000/µL (normal 150,000 to 400,000/µL); counts below 20,000/µL are unusual, which is one reason bleeding is uncommon. Venous thrombosis (deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism) is more frequent than arterial thrombosis (limb ischemia, stroke, myocardial infarction), and skin necrosis at injection sites and adrenal hemorrhage from adrenal vein thrombosis can occur.

Risk is higher with unfractionated heparin than with low molecular weight heparin, because longer chains bridge more PF4 molecules and form the large complexes that are most antigenic, and higher after cardiac and orthopedic surgery than in medical patients. HIT must be distinguished from nonimmune heparin-associated thrombocytopenia, a mild fall in the first 1 to 2 days caused by a direct effect of heparin on platelets, which recovers despite continued heparin and carries no thrombotic risk. Laboratory testing reflects the mechanism: an immunoassay for anti-PF4 and heparin antibodies is sensitive but detects many antibodies that do not activate platelets, while a functional assay that measures platelet activation (serotonin release) is more specific.

blocks.predict: Why would a patient with a platelet count of 60,000/µL from HIT have a thrombosis rather than bleeding?
blocks.explain: The count is low because platelets are being activated and consumed in clots and cleared after antibody coating. Activated platelets, microparticles, monocyte tissue factor, and endothelial injury generate thrombin, and 60,000/µL is still enough for hemostasis.

blocks.text: Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) is an autoimmune disorder defined by persistent antiphospholipid antibodies together with thrombosis or pregnancy morbidity. Despite the name, the main targets are proteins that bind anionic phospholipid, chiefly beta2 glycoprotein I and prothrombin. Three laboratory measures are used: lupus anticoagulant (a functional clotting test), anticardiolipin antibodies, and anti-beta2 glycoprotein I antibodies (both immunoassays). APS can be primary or secondary, most often to SLE, and the antibodies must be present on two occasions at least 12 weeks apart, because transient antibodies follow many infections.
Why the PTT is prolonged in the tube

The tenase and prothrombinase complexes assemble on a phospholipid surface. The PTT reagent supplies only a limited amount of phospholipid, and antibodies that bind beta2 glycoprotein I or prothrombin on that surface occupy it and block the complexes. The PTT, and especially the more sensitive dilute Russell viper venom time, is prolonged. A mixing study with normal plasma does not correct it, which shows an inhibitor rather than a factor deficiency, and adding excess phospholipid does correct it, which confirms that the inhibitor is phospholipid dependent. The PT is usually normal because its thromboplastin reagent contains abundant phospholipid.

blocks.title: Same antibody, opposite effects
steps: Antibody binds beta2 glycoprotein I on phospholipid
In the tube: scarce reagent phospholipid is blocked
Clotting complexes cannot assemble; PTT prolonged
In the body: phospholipid surfaces are abundant
Antibody cross-links beta2 glycoprotein I on cells
Endothelium, monocytes, platelets, complement activated; thrombosis
blocks.caption: A laboratory artifact of limited phospholipid hides a strongly procoagulant effect in vivo.

blocks.text: In the body, membranes provide abundant phospholipid, so the anticoagulant effect is irrelevant. Antibodies instead cross-link beta2 glycoprotein I bound to cell surfaces and signal through cell receptors. Endothelial cells express tissue factor and adhesion molecules, monocytes express tissue factor, platelets become activated, and complement is activated, with C5a amplifying inflammation. The antibodies also impair natural anticoagulant defenses, including the protein C pathway and the annexin A5 shield that normally covers phospholipid on placental surfaces, and they reduce fibrinolysis. Because this acts on any vessel, APS causes both venous thrombosis (deep vein thrombosis is most common) and arterial thrombosis (stroke and transient ischemic attack), an unusual combination that points to the diagnosis.

Pregnancy loss reflects placental thrombosis and infarction, impaired trophoblast invasion, and complement-mediated inflammation at the maternal and fetal interface. Recognized pregnancy morbidity includes unexplained fetal death at or after 10 weeks, premature birth before 34 weeks from severe preeclampsia or placental insufficiency, and three or more unexplained consecutive losses before 10 weeks. Other findings explained by the antibodies are mild thrombocytopenia, livedo reticularis, and a false-positive nontreponemal syphilis test, because the RPR and VDRL antigen contains cardiolipin.

blocks.predict: A patient's PTT is prolonged and does not correct with a 1:1 mix of normal plasma. Should you expect bleeding?
blocks.explain: Not necessarily. Failure to correct means an inhibitor. If it is a lupus anticoagulant, the risk is thrombosis, because the antibody blocks only the scarce phospholipid in the reagent and activates cells in vivo. A factor VIII inhibitor would instead cause bleeding, which is why the clinical picture and phospholipid-dependent tests are needed.
blocks.check: Why the PTT is prolonged in the tube.

blocks.text: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV, human herpesvirus 4) is an enveloped double-stranded DNA herpesvirus spread by saliva. It replicates in oropharyngeal epithelium and infects B cells in the tonsils. Its envelope glycoprotein gp350 binds CD21, also called complement receptor 2 (CR2), the B cell receptor for the complement fragment C3d, and glycoprotein gp42 binds HLA class II to complete entry. The virus then establishes lifelong latency in memory B cells as a circular episome.

Latent EBV proteins make infected B cells proliferate. EBNA-1 maintains the viral genome in dividing cells, EBNA-2 drives B cell growth genes, latent membrane protein 1 (LMP1) mimics a constitutively active CD40 receptor and activates NF-kappa B, and LMP2A mimics B cell receptor signaling. These are the same signals a B cell normally receives from T cell help and antigen, delivered without either.

blocks.title: From EBV infection to mononucleosis
steps: Saliva exposure; virus replicates in pharyngeal epithelium
gp350 binds CD21 on tonsillar B cells
Latent proteins drive polyclonal B cell proliferation
CD8 T cells expand to kill infected B cells
Atypical lymphocytes, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, pharyngitis
Infection controlled; lifelong latency in memory B cells
blocks.caption: Most symptoms of mononucleosis come from the T cell response, not from direct viral damage.

blocks.text: Infectious mononucleosis occurs mainly in adolescents and young adults, whose primary infection provokes a vigorous response. CD8 cytotoxic T cells expand massively against the infected B cells; these activated T cells are the atypical lymphocytes (large cells with abundant cytoplasm that indents around neighboring red cells), and the infected B cells are a small minority. Lymphoid hyperplasia causes fever, exudative pharyngitis, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly, with a risk of splenic rupture, and mild hepatitis is common. Polyclonal B cell activation produces heterophile antibodies (IgM that agglutinates sheep or horse red cells, the basis of the Monospot test), which may be absent early and in young children, and cold agglutinins with anti-i specificity.

blocks.title: EBV-associated lymphoid neoplasms

Nearly all EBV positive; MYC translocation, usually t(8;14), is the essential event; Plasmodium falciparum malaria drives B cell expansion and weakens T cell control
Abdominal masses in Western countries; HIV
A minority of sporadic cases EBV positive; MYC translocation is still required
EBV in Reed-Sternberg cells in a large fraction; LMP1 supplies NF-kappa B survival signals
Organ or stem cell transplant with T cell immunosuppression
Unrestrained EBV-driven B cell growth, often with full latent protein expression
Primary CNS lymphoma is almost always EBV positive; also diffuse large B cell lymphoma
blocks.caption: EBV contributes to lymphoma when cofactors add genetic hits or when T cell surveillance fails.

blocks.text: EBV is necessary for transformation in some settings but not sufficient. In Burkitt lymphoma the virus and chronic malaria expand the pool of proliferating B cells, raising the chance of an error during class switching or somatic hypermutation that moves MYC next to an immunoglobulin gene. In immunosuppressed patients the problem is loss of CD8 T cell surveillance, so infected B cells expressing the growth program are no longer removed. EBV is also linked to nasopharyngeal carcinoma, an epithelial tumor.

sections.title: Asplenia and infection by encapsulated bacteria

blocks.text: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib), and Neisseria meningitidis are covered by a polysaccharide capsule. The capsule is hydrophilic and negatively charged, hides surface ligands from phagocyte receptors, and limits deposition of C3b; most meningococcal capsules, for example, contain sialic acid, which recruits the complement regulator factor H. These bacteria are therefore cleared efficiently only after they are opsonized by antibody and complement.

The spleen is built for this task. In the red pulp, blood flows slowly through the cords past macrophages before squeezing back into the sinusoids, so poorly opsonized bacteria are captured that the liver, with its faster flow, would miss. The marginal zone between red and white pulp contains B cells that respond to polysaccharides without T cell help and rapidly secrete IgM, which activates complement and opsonizes with C3b. The spleen is also an important site of early antibody production after bloodstream exposure.

blocks.title: What the spleen contributes and what loss of it shows
rows: Removes poorly opsonized bacteria and parasitized red cells
Fulminant bacteremia; severe babesiosis and malaria
Weak early antibody to encapsulated bacteria
Pitting and culling of red cells
Removes nuclear remnants and inclusions; destroys old cells
Howell-Jolly bodies, target cells, Pappenheimer bodies
Holds about one third of platelets
blocks.caption: Blood smear changes reveal asplenia even when the history does not.

blocks.text: Without a spleen, bacteria that are poorly opsonized multiply in the blood, and overwhelming post-splenectomy infection can progress within hours from fever to septic shock and DIC. S. pneumoniae causes most cases. Risk is greatest in young children and in the first years after splenectomy but is lifelong. Asplenia may be surgical (trauma, hereditary spherocytosis) or functional. In sickle cell anemia, sickled cells repeatedly occlude the slow splenic circulation, causing infarction and fibrosis; function is lost in early childhood, and the scarred, shrunken organ is called autosplenectomy. Howell-Jolly bodies on the smear of a child with sickle cell disease signal this loss.
Why vaccination protects

A plain capsular polysaccharide is a T-independent antigen: its repeating units cross-link B cell receptors and produce mainly IgM, with little class switching, affinity maturation, or memory, and children under about 2 years respond poorly because their marginal zone is immature. Conjugate vaccines attach the polysaccharide to a carrier protein. The resulting IgG opsonizes the capsule and activates complement, so the bacteria can be cleared by macrophages in the liver and elsewhere without the spleen, and memory B cells allow a rapid response on exposure.

blocks.title: How a conjugate vaccine recruits T cell help
steps: B cell receptor binds capsular polysaccharide
B cell internalizes the attached carrier protein
Carrier peptides presented on MHC class II
Carrier-specific CD4 T cell gives CD40 ligand and cytokines
Germinal center: class switch to IgG, affinity maturation
Memory B cells and long-lived plasma cells against the capsule
blocks.caption: The T cell recognizes the protein, but the antibody is directed at the polysaccharide (linked recognition).

integration.text: Immunology supplies the rules, and the blood disorders apply them. Antibody class decides location and effector: IgG engages Fc receptors on splenic macrophages (warm AIHA, delayed hemolytic reaction) or on platelets (HIT), while pentameric IgM fixes complement and lyses cells in the circulation (acute hemolytic reaction, cold agglutinins). The same Fc receptor that clears coated red cells activates coated platelets, which is why one disease destroys cells and the other builds clots. Antigen location separates type II from type III, so cryoglobulins damage vessels and kidneys rather than the cells they began on.

Microbiology and pathology meet in the spleen and in B cells. Mycoplasma and EBV trigger cold agglutinins through molecular mimicry and polyclonal B cell activation; EBV hijacks B cell growth signals and, when T cell control fails or malaria adds proliferative pressure, contributes to lymphoma; and splenic loss in sickle cell disease removes the main defense against encapsulated bacteria. Laboratory tests must be read with their limits in mind: a positive direct Coombs test shows coating, not necessarily hemolysis, PF4 antibody immunoassays detect antibodies that may not activate platelets, and a prolonged PTT from lupus anticoagulant signals thrombosis, not bleeding.

summary: Warm AIHA is IgG at 37 °C (98.6 °F): splenic Fc receptor phagocytosis, spherocytes, extravascular hemolysis, direct Coombs IgG positive; associated with SLE, CLL, and drugs.
Cold agglutinin disease is IgM binding below about 30 °C (86 °F): agglutination and complement, C3 only on direct Coombs; associated with Mycoplasma (anti-I), EBV (anti-i), and clonal B cell disease.
The direct Coombs test detects IgG or C3 already on red cells; the indirect test detects free antibody in serum, as in screens and crossmatches.

Acute hemolytic transfusion reactions, AIHA, and hemolytic disease of the newborn are type II; mixed cryoglobulinemia with low C4, purpura, and glomerulonephritis, usually from hepatitis C, is type III.

Transfusion reactions sort by timing and hemolysis: acute hemolytic in minutes, anaphylactic (anti-IgA) in seconds without fever, TRALI within 6 hours, febrile nonhemolytic within hours, delayed hemolytic in about 3 to 10 days.
In HIT, IgG against heparin and PF4 cross-links platelet Fc gamma RIIa, activating platelets; counts fall more than 50% at 5 to 10 days and thrombosis, mostly venous, results.

Antiphospholipid antibodies prolong the PTT in vitro by blocking scarce reagent phospholipid but activate endothelium, monocytes, platelets, and complement in vivo, causing venous and arterial thrombosis and pregnancy loss.
EBV enters B cells through CD21; atypical lymphocytes in mononucleosis are CD8 T cells; EBV contributes to endemic Burkitt, Hodgkin, and immunosuppression-related lymphomas.

Asplenia, surgical or from sickle cell autosplenectomy, allows sepsis from S. pneumoniae, Hib, and N. meningitidis; conjugate vaccines convert a T-independent polysaccharide response into T-dependent IgG and memory.

verify: Thermal thresholds for cold agglutinins (binding below about 30 °C (86 °F), strongest near 4 °C (39 °F)) are approximate and vary with the antibody's thermal amplitude.
The proportion of idiopathic warm AIHA (about half here) varies among sources from roughly 40% to 60%.

Delayed hemolytic reaction timing is given as about 3 to 10 days here; some sources extend it to 14 days or more. Febrile nonhemolytic timing (within about 4 hours) follows hemovigilance definitions that vary between agencies.
Mechanism of anaphylactic reactions in IgA deficiency: the anti-IgA antibodies are often IgG, and the exact mediator pathway is debated; confirm the wording NABNE expects.

HIT values (onset 5 to 10 days, rapid onset with heparin within about 100 days, median nadir about 50,000 to 60,000/µL) are consensus figures; confirm whether NABNE Part I expects the 4Ts clinical score.
APS criteria in this chapter follow the revised Sapporo (Sydney) criteria; the 2023 ACR and EULAR classification criteria use a weighted point system. Confirm which set NABNE uses.

The fraction of EBV-positive cases in sporadic Burkitt lymphoma (often quoted near 15% to 30%) and classical Hodgkin lymphoma (often quoted near 40% overall, higher in mixed cellularity) varies by region and source; this chapter avoids exact figures.
The age at which functional asplenia and autosplenectomy develop in sickle cell anemia is given as early childhood; sources range from the first year of life to about age 5.
Confirm whether NABNE expects the term hemolytic disease of the newborn or hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn, and whether eponyms such as Downey cells are tested.
